description: Day-to-day friction experienced by people with ADHD, autism, dyslexia, blindness or low vision, deafness or hearing loss, mobility or motor impairments, and executive-function difficulties, where software could remove or reduce the barrier.

items.title: Reminders that get dismissed and forgotten
items.problem: A phone reminder fires while you are mid-task, you swipe it away intending to act later, and it is gone from your mind within seconds.
items.who: adults with ADHD
items.workaround: Setting five duplicate alarms or leaving the reminder unread on purpose

items.title: Time blindness before appointments
items.problem: You cannot feel how much time is left before you need to leave, so you are either 40 minutes early or 20 minutes late, with nothing in between.
items.who: people with ADHD
items.workaround: Multiple countdown alarms, visual timers, asking a partner to nudge

items.title: Task initiation paralysis on simple chores
items.problem: Knowing exactly what needs doing but being unable to start, even a two-minute task, and feeling shame that grows the longer it sits.
items.who: adults with ADHD, autistic adults, people with depression
items.workaround: Body doubling over video, bargaining with oneself, waiting for a deadline panic

items.title: Finding a body double on demand
items.problem: Working alongside another person helps you focus, but there is nobody available right when you need to start, and scheduling a session is itself a task.
items.who: remote workers and students with ADHD
items.workaround: Discord study rooms, Focusmate, calling a friend

items.title: Hyperfocus erases meals and breaks
items.problem: You look up from a task and six hours have passed without eating, drinking, or moving, and you now feel awful.
items.who: people with ADHD and autistic adults
items.workaround: Interval alarms that get ignored

items.title: Forgetting whether medication was taken
items.problem: Twenty minutes after your morning routine you cannot remember whether you took your stimulant, and doubling up or skipping both have real consequences.
items.who: people on daily ADHD or psychiatric medication
items.workaround: Pill organizers, photographing the bottle, counting remaining pills

items.title: Controlled-substance refill timing chaos
items.problem: Stimulant prescriptions cannot be refilled early, pharmacies are frequently out of stock, and tracking the earliest refill date and which pharmacy has supply becomes a monthly scramble.
items.who: adults and parents managing ADHD medication
items.workaround: Calling pharmacies one by one, calendar notes, Reddit shortage threads

items.title: Abandoned to-do apps graveyard
items.problem: Every task app works for two weeks, then the novelty fades, the list becomes a wall of overdue red, and opening it feels like being scolded.
items.who: adults with ADHD
items.workaround: Switching apps, paper lists, sticky notes on the monitor

items.title: Out of sight, out of mind items
items.problem: Anything put in a drawer, cupboard or folder effectively ceases to exist, leading to duplicate purchases, expired food and missed paperwork.
items.who: people with ADHD
items.workaround: Clear bins, leaving everything on surfaces, labeling

items.title: Emotional dysregulation after minor setbacks
items.problem: A small piece of criticism or a perceived rejection triggers an outsized emotional crash that wipes out the rest of the day's plans.
items.who: adults with ADHD (rejection sensitivity)
items.workaround: Therapy skills, venting to friends, avoidance

items.title: Reading long emails and losing the ask
items.problem: A dense email or Slack thread contains one actual request buried in paragraphs, and you skim, miss it, and get chased later.
items.who: workers with ADHD or dyslexia
items.workaround: Asking the sender to bullet it, re-reading three times

items.title: Transition between tasks feels impossible
items.problem: Stopping one activity to begin another, even a pleasant one, produces disproportionate resistance and the change gets delayed for hours.
items.who: autistic adults and people with ADHD
items.workaround: Advance warnings, rigid schedules, timers with escalating alerts

items.title: Breaking big tasks into steps
items.problem: A project like 'sort out taxes' has no obvious first step, so it stays on the list for months while the deadline creeps closer.
items.who: adults with ADHD and executive-function difficulties
items.workaround: Asking a friend to talk it through, AI chat prompts

items.title: Doom piles and doom boxes
items.problem: Miscellaneous items get dumped in a pile or box 'to deal with later', and the pile grows until sorting it becomes overwhelming.
items.who: people with ADHD
items.workaround: Periodic purges, moving the box to another room

items.title: Sensory overload in shops and transit
items.problem: Fluorescent lights, background music, crowds and announcements stack up until you have to leave a supermarket mid-shop or miss your stop.
items.who: autistic adults, people with sensory processing differences
items.workaround: Noise-cancelling headphones, sunglasses, shopping at odd hours

items.title: Unknown sensory environment of new venues
items.problem: Before visiting a restaurant, clinic or venue you cannot find out how loud, bright or crowded it is, so you either avoid it or risk a meltdown.
items.who: autistic people and parents of autistic children
items.workaround: Phoning ahead, checking photos, arriving at opening time

items.title: Phone calls required for basic services
items.problem: Doctors, landlords and utilities insist on phone calls, and the unpredictability of live conversation causes hours of dread and postponed tasks.
items.who: autistic adults, people with anxiety, deaf and hard-of-hearing people
items.workaround: Scripting the call, asking a family member to call, avoiding the task

items.title: Decoding tone in text messages
items.problem: A short reply like 'ok.' or 'fine' can be read as anger or dismissal, leading to hours of rumination about whether someone is upset.
items.who: autistic adults, people with rejection sensitivity
items.workaround: Asking directly, screenshotting to friends for a second opinion, tone indicators

items.title: Unwritten social scripts for common situations
items.problem: Interactions like checking into a hotel, small talk with a barber or declining an invitation have unstated expectations that must be worked out from scratch each time.
items.who: autistic adults
items.workaround: Memorized scripts, rehearsing, watching how others do it

items.title: Unexpected plan changes derail the day
items.problem: A cancelled appointment or a friend arriving late throws off a carefully structured day and the fallout can last hours.
items.who: autistic adults and children
items.workaround: Backup plans, over-communicating, avoiding plans with unreliable people

items.title: Visual schedules that don't update
items.problem: Printed picture schedules for a child fall out of date the moment plans change, and remaking them with laminated cards is slow.
items.who: parents and teachers of autistic children
items.workaround: Velcro card boards, whiteboards, printing new cards

items.title: Going nonverbal with no quick way to communicate
items.problem: During shutdown or overload speech becomes unavailable, and there is no fast way to tell people around you what is happening or what you need.
items.who: autistic people with intermittent speech
items.workaround: Pre-written cards, typing in Notes and showing the screen

items.title: Interoception blind spots
items.problem: Not noticing hunger, thirst, tiredness or needing the toilet until it becomes urgent or turns into a headache and irritability.
items.who: autistic adults, people with ADHD
items.workaround: Scheduled eating and drinking, tracking apps

items.title: Masking exhaustion goes untracked
items.problem: After a day of performing neurotypical behavior you crash, but the link between specific social loads and the burnout is invisible until it is too late.
items.who: autistic adults, especially late-diagnosed
items.workaround: Energy accounting ('spoons'), cancelling plans reactively

items.title: Safe foods running out
items.problem: A narrow set of tolerated foods means a discontinued product, recipe change or empty shelf can leave nothing acceptable to eat.
items.who: autistic people and those with ARFID
items.workaround: Stockpiling, checking multiple stores, eating nothing

items.title: Reading on screens with dense text
items.problem: Long paragraphs in small fonts on white backgrounds cause letters to swim and lines to be re-read, so articles and documentation take three times longer.
items.who: people with dyslexia and visual stress
items.workaround: Browser reader mode, overlays, text-to-speech, giving up

items.title: Spellcheck can't guess dyslexic spellings
items.problem: When a word is spelled phonetically or with letters transposed, standard spellcheck offers no useful suggestion, and searching for the word also fails.
items.who: people with dyslexia
items.workaround: Voice dictation, asking someone, describing the word to a search engine

items.title: Paper forms at clinics and offices
items.problem: Handwritten forms in waiting rooms must be filled in under time pressure with no spellcheck or dictation, causing embarrassment and errors.
items.who: people with dyslexia or dysgraphia, people with tremor
items.workaround: Bringing a companion, asking for the form in advance, leaving fields blank

items.title: Scanned PDFs that can't be read aloud
items.problem: Work and school documents arrive as image-only PDFs that text-to-speech tools cannot read, so the content is locked away.
items.who: students and workers with dyslexia, blind and low-vision users
items.workaround: Running OCR manually, asking for an accessible version, skipping the reading

items.title: Mixing up similar-looking numbers
items.problem: Transposing digits in phone numbers, bank details or dates leads to failed payments and missed appointments, and the error is hard to spot on review.
items.who: people with dyscalculia or dyslexia
items.workaround: Copy-paste only, reading numbers aloud, asking someone to double check

items.title: Reading aloud in meetings or class
items.problem: Being asked to read a passage aloud on the spot causes panic and stumbling, and there is no discreet way to preview or get support.
items.who: students and employees with dyslexia
items.workaround: Pre-reading, declining, disclosing the disability

items.title: Unlabeled buttons in apps
items.problem: Screen readers announce 'button, button, button' because icons have no labels, making core features of mainstream apps unusable.
items.who: blind and low-vision smartphone users
items.workaround: Guessing by position, asking sighted help, emailing developers

items.title: Images and memes with no alt text
items.problem: Friends share screenshots and memes in group chats and social feeds that arrive as silent 'image' to a screen reader, leaving you out of the conversation.
items.who: blind and low-vision social media users
items.workaround: Asking what the picture is, AI image description tools

items.title: Identifying cans and packages in the kitchen
items.problem: Cans, boxes and jars feel identical, and printed labels and cooking instructions are unreadable without sighted assistance.
items.who: blind and low-vision people cooking at home
items.workaround: Braille or rubber-band labeling systems, barcode scanning apps, memorizing shelf positions

items.title: Touchscreen appliances and kiosks
items.problem: Flat touchscreen microwaves, washing machines, self-checkouts and ticket kiosks give no tactile or audio feedback, so they cannot be operated independently.
items.who: blind and low-vision people
items.workaround: Tactile bump stickers, memorizing button sequences, asking staff

items.title: Finding the entrance and the right door
items.problem: GPS gets you to the address but not to the actual door, and once inside there is no way to find the reception desk, the right room or the toilet.
items.who: blind and low-vision people navigating alone
items.workaround: Asking passers-by, remote sighted assistance apps, arriving early

items.title: Which bus is this at the stop
items.problem: Several buses arrive at once and there is no audio announcement of the route number, so you may board the wrong one or miss yours.
items.who: blind and low-vision transit riders
items.workaround: Asking the driver, asking others at the stop, live vehicle tracking apps

items.title: Reading mail and bills that arrive on paper
items.problem: Letters, bills and official notices come in print and must be photographed and OCR'd one page at a time, or wait for a sighted person.
items.who: blind and low-vision adults
items.workaround: Phone camera OCR apps, family reading it, requesting large print or email

items.title: Matching clothes and checking for stains
items.problem: Choosing an outfit that matches and is clean requires colour and stain information that is not available by touch.
items.who: blind and colour-blind people
items.workaround: Colour identifier apps, buying only neutral colours, labeling hangers

items.title: Inaccessible CAPTCHAs block sign-ups
items.problem: Image-based CAPTCHAs have no working audio alternative or the audio is unintelligible, so you cannot create accounts or log in.
items.who: blind users and people with cognitive disabilities
items.workaround: Asking sighted help, browser extensions, abandoning the site

items.title: Low-contrast text and thin fonts
items.problem: Light grey text on white and hairline fonts are unreadable even with zoom, and zooming breaks layouts so buttons disappear off screen.
items.who: low-vision and older users
items.workaround: High-contrast modes, browser zoom, reader view, custom CSS

items.title: Group conversations in noisy restaurants
items.problem: Following several people talking over background noise is impossible, so you nod along and miss the plans being made.
items.who: deaf and hard-of-hearing people, people with auditory processing disorder
items.workaround: Live transcription apps, sitting with your back to the wall, leaving early

items.title: Videos and live streams without captions
items.problem: Social media videos, online courses and workplace recordings often have no captions or auto-captions so wrong they are useless.
items.who: deaf and hard-of-hearing people
items.workaround: Requesting transcripts, third-party captioning tools, skipping the content

items.title: Missing doorbells, alarms and announcements
items.problem: Deliveries are missed because the doorbell is not heard, and airport or train platform changes are announced only by loudspeaker.
items.who: deaf and hard-of-hearing people
items.workaround: Flashing-light doorbells, watching departure boards constantly, asking staff

items.title: Businesses that only take phone bookings
items.problem: Clinics, restaurants and tradespeople with no online booking or text option are effectively closed to you, or require a relay service that many hang up on.
items.who: deaf people and non-speaking people
items.workaround: Relay services, asking a hearing friend, choosing only businesses with online booking

items.title: Drive-throughs and intercoms
items.problem: Ordering at drive-throughs, buzzing into apartment buildings and speaking to parking-garage intercoms all depend on hearing a crackly speaker.
items.who: deaf and hard-of-hearing people
items.workaround: Going inside, pre-written cards, mobile ordering apps

items.title: Hearing-aid battery and connectivity failures
items.problem: Rechargeable hearing aids die mid-day, Bluetooth pairing drops, and there is no warning until conversation suddenly vanishes.
items.who: hearing-aid and cochlear-implant users
items.workaround: Carrying spare batteries, restarting the phone, manufacturer apps

items.title: Video calls with fast-talking colleagues
items.problem: Meeting captions lag, speakers talk over each other, and lipreading fails when cameras are off, so you leave meetings unsure what was decided.
items.who: deaf and hard-of-hearing remote workers
items.workaround: Asking for written summaries, recording and re-watching, live captioners

items.title: Step-free route unknown before travel
items.problem: Map apps route you via stairs, broken lifts and kerbs without dropped curbs, and you only discover it when you are stuck in front of them.
items.who: wheelchair users, people with mobility impairments, parents with prams
items.workaround: Street View scouting, phoning venues, transit lift-status pages

items.title: Accessible toilet location and access
items.problem: Finding an accessible toilet nearby, knowing whether it is locked, needs a key, or is being used as storage, is a constant unknown when out.
items.who: wheelchair users and people with continence conditions
items.workaround: Radar key schemes, crowd-sourced toilet maps, limiting fluid intake

items.title: Venue 'accessible' claims that are wrong
items.problem: Restaurants and hotels say they are accessible, but there is a step at the door, the lift is tiny or the accessible room has a bathtub.
items.who: wheelchair users and people with limited mobility
items.workaround: Calling to ask specific questions, asking for photos, relying on word of mouth

items.title: Blocked accessible parking and ramps
items.problem: Disabled bays are taken by non-permit cars and ramps are blocked by bins or delivery vans, and reporting it is slow or pointless.
items.who: disabled drivers and wheelchair users
items.workaround: Driving around, confronting drivers, reporting to the council

items.title: Tiny touch targets and precise gestures
items.problem: Small buttons, swipe-to-delete gestures and drag-and-drop are error-prone with tremor or limited dexterity, leading to accidental taps and sends.
items.who: people with tremor, arthritis, cerebral palsy or motor impairments
items.workaround: Styluses, accessibility touch settings, voice control, asking someone

items.title: Voice control fails in web forms
items.problem: Dictation and voice navigation work in some fields but not others, so a form has to be abandoned halfway or completed by someone else.
items.who: people with limited hand use who rely on voice input
items.workaround: Switching devices, browser extensions, asking for assistance

items.title: Booking wheelchair-accessible taxis
items.problem: Ride-hailing apps rarely have accessible vehicles available, wait times are far longer, and drivers sometimes cancel on seeing a wheelchair.
items.who: wheelchair users
items.workaround: Booking hours ahead, local taxi firms, paratransit schemes

items.title: Energy budgeting on bad pain days
items.problem: Not knowing how much energy tomorrow will hold means over-committing and then cancelling everything, or under-committing and losing days.
items.who: people with chronic pain, fatigue or mobility conditions
items.workaround: Spoon theory tracking, pacing diaries, keeping days empty

items.title: Requesting accommodations is unclear
items.problem: Working out what you are entitled to at work or university, how to word the request and what documentation is needed takes weeks of research and emails.
items.who: neurodivergent and disabled students and employees
items.workaround: Advocacy groups, templates from forums, asking others who have done it

items.title: Explaining a condition to every new person
items.problem: Each new doctor, teacher or manager needs the same explanation of how your condition affects you and what helps, and it is exhausting to repeat.
items.who: neurodivergent and disabled people, parents of disabled children
items.workaround: Prepared 'about me' documents, hospital passports, memorized speech

items.title: Coordinating a child's therapy schedule
items.problem: Speech, occupational and behavioral therapy sessions, school meetings and specialist appointments overlap and change, with paperwork from each provider.
items.who: parents of autistic or disabled children
items.workaround: Shared calendars, binders, spreadsheets

items.title: Screen-reader friendliness of a site unknown
items.problem: Before spending time on a new shop or service you cannot tell whether checkout will work with assistive tech, and you often find out at the last step.
items.who: screen reader and keyboard-only users
items.workaround: Community recommendations, trial and error, sticking to known sites

items.title: Waiting-room and queue uncertainty
items.problem: Sitting in an unpredictable waiting room with no idea how long it will be is distressing, and stepping out to regulate risks losing your place.
items.who: autistic people, people with anxiety, people with ADHD
items.workaround: Asking reception repeatedly, waiting in the car, headphones

items.title: Keeping routines during travel
items.problem: Hotels, time zones and unfamiliar shops break carefully built medication, meal and sleep routines, and the disruption takes days to recover from.
items.who: autistic people, people with ADHD, people on strict medication schedules
items.workaround: Packing lists, bringing safe foods, extra alarms

items.title: Autoplay and flashing content triggers
items.problem: Autoplaying videos, animated ads and flashing effects cause distraction, migraines or seizures, and per-site settings do not persist.
items.who: people with ADHD, photosensitive epilepsy, vestibular disorders
items.workaround: Browser extensions, reduced-motion settings, avoiding sites
